newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani papers say Gujral dampens peace hopes.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani papers say Gujral dampens peace hopes.

text.p: Pakistani newspapers said on Tuesday India's new Prime Minister, Inder Kumar Gujral, had dampened peace hopes in remarks on Kashmir.

"Some of the optimism, if not euphoria, expressed in the country at (Gujral's) appointment should be tempered by some of the remarks that he has just made during a visit to Jammu in occupied Kashmir," the English-language Dawn newspaper said.
While in Jammu, Gujral said he had no plans to meet leaders of the All Jammu and Kashmir Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, representing political and militant groups opposed to Indian rule.

Pakistani papers quoted him as saying last year's state elections had ended the Kashmir issue. "Kashmir is no longer an issue. Where is the issue as elections have been held and an elected government has been installed in Kashmir?" he was quoted as saying.
Pakistan and India have fought two wars over Kashmir since both countries gained independence from Britain in 1947.
India controls two-thirds of the region while Pakistan controls the remaining one third.
Dawn said niceties expressed by Gujral after becoming prime minister did not mean he would be swayed by emotions.

"A man of peace he may be, but prime ministers anywhere in the world... want peace on their own terms," it said. "Which is what, it is utterly safe to assume, Mr Gujral would want in occupied Kashmir: peace but on India's terms."
Dawn said India-Pakistan talks, which resumed in March after a three-year break, were a positive step, but could be meaningful only if the Kashmir dispute was on the table.
The Nation daily said Gujral's remarks in Jammu were important because they flew in the face of what Pakistan's prime minister and foreign minister had been saying on the subject.

"The strangeness of this visit and the whole show put up in Jammu needs to be noted by our Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub, who appeared so euphoric after his visit to India and who has again pointed to Kashmir being at the core of talks," it said.
The News said Gujral's statement should serve as a warning to Islamabad, despite his vows to improve ties with Pakistan.

His appointment as prime minister had created hopes for moderate elements in both countries, the newspaper said. But Gujral, "like his predecessors, has dutifully reiterated what his country's leaders have been saying all along".
"Gujral needs to realise that, even if the hardline elements have to be pacified, he ought not to make statements that could sabotage the entire normalisation process," The News said.

Gujral is due to meet Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Maldives in May. As foreign minister under the previous Indian government, he met Ayub at a Non-Aligned Movement meeting in Delhi this month.
The Frontier Post said Gujral's statement seemed destined to abort the rapprochement begun last month. "Therefore, for all practical purposes, things appear to be back to square one."
The daily said that "sham elections" in Indian-controlled Jammu and Kashmir had no relevance to the Kashmir dispute.

"It can only be resolved through a U.N.-supervised plebiscite," The Frontier Post said, referring to Islamabad's demand for mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
